pl-l4d50c7-d1e115.summary: Finally asks whether the sight of the reprobate's punishment discolors the glory of the blessed or benefits their beatitude.

pl-l4d50c7-d1e118.summary: Quotes Gregory: the sight of the reprobate's punishment does not darken the beatitude of the just, since where there is no compassion for misery it cannot lessen the joy of the blessed; though their own joys suffice them, they see, for greater glory, the punishments of the wicked which they escaped by grace, since those who see God's brightness can see whatever happens in creation.
claims: The sight of punishment does not lessen beatitude.
It increases glory by showing what grace saved them from.

pl-l4d50c7-d1e127.summary: Continues: it is not surprising that immortal saints see the reprobate with the understanding, since mortal prophets were granted to see all this; the elect will go out, not in place but in understanding or clear vision, to see the torments of the impious, not affected with grief but filled with joy, giving thanks for their deliverance at the sight of the impious' unspeakable calamity.
claims: The blessed see the damned by understanding.
They rejoice and give thanks for their deliverance.

pl-l4d50c7-d1e134.summary: Cites Isaiah describing the torments of the impious and the joy of the good: the elect will go out and see the corpses of those who transgressed against me; their worm will not die nor their fire be quenched, and they will be a sight to all flesh, the elect; the just will rejoice when he sees vengeance.
claims: The just rejoice at the sight of divine justice.

pl-l4d50c7-d1e146.summary: An apparent fragment or heading, 'Exultativa operis', marking the work's closing.

pl-l4d50c7-d1e149.summary: Closes the whole work: it suffices for the writer, if not the hearer, to have recalled these things about the feet of him who sits on the high throne, which the Seraphim covered with two wings; having begun from the face of the one seated, he has come through the middle to the feet, with the Way as guide.
claims: The work has passed from God's face through the middle to his feet.
Christ, the Way, has guided the work.

pl-l4d50c7.summary: Finally asks whether the sight of the reprobate's punishment darkens or adds to the glory of the blessed. Gregory: it does not darken it, since without compassion it cannot lessen their joy; though their own joys suffice, seeing the punishments they escaped by grace increases their glory, since those who see God's brightness can see anything in creation. The elect will go out not in place but in understanding to see the torments of the impious, not grieving but rejoicing and giving thanks for their deliverance, as Isaiah says, 'the just will rejoice when he sees vengeance'. Lombard closes the work: having begun from the face of him who sits on the throne, he has come through the middle to the feet, the Way leading.
claims: Seeing the damned does not lessen the joy of the blessed.
It increases their gratitude for deliverance by grace.
The work concludes, having passed from God through the middle to the last things.
